cases.name: 01-windows-bash-grant-wasted-judges
cases.promptMarkdown:
I'm testing my plugin `tidy-notes` on my Windows 11 laptop (Claude Code 2.1.312, native Windows, no WSL installed, Max subscription). The skill normalises a notes file by running a small Python script through Bash and then writing the cleaned file back. From the plugin root I ran:

```
claude plugin eval . --runs 3 --judge-model sonnet --allow-tools Bash Write Edit -j 4
```

Near the top of the output there was an "access is denied" line mentioning `C:\Windows\System32\config\systemprofile\AppData\Local\Microsoft\WindowsApps`. Then every progress line, WITH and W/OUT alike, ended with an error saying the run was refused because no sandbox backend is available on this platform. Summary:

```
CASE             WITH  W/OUT Δ      RUNS COST   NOTES
normalise-basic  0.00  0.00  +0.00  6    $0.83  run refused: no sandbox backend
dedupe-headers   0.00  0.00  +0.00  6    $0.81  run refused: no sandbox backend
keep-frontmatter 0.00  0.00  +0.00  6    $0.85  run refused: no sandbox backend

3 case(s) · mean Δ +0.00 · 95s · $2.49
```

Each case has two `llm` graders and one `tool_used` grader. No agent run did anything, yet it reports $2.49 and my plan usage dropped.

I have a Linux cloud box available tomorrow. Please tell me: (1) why there is a cost when nothing ran, (2) the exact command to run on this PC tonight so I don't burn usage for nothing again, (3) what to run on the Linux box and the setup it needs, and (4) what to expect from the skill's file-writing step even once the shell works there.

graders.name: cost-real-judges-ran
graders.graderMarkdown:
The user asks why $2.49 was reported and plan usage dropped although no agent run did anything. A correct reply must say the cost is real usage because the `llm` judge graders still ran (and were counted) on runs that produced nothing, so a shell grant on native Windows spends usage for zero information.

PASS: The reply explains that the $2.49 is real plan usage consumed by the judge (llm grader) calls, which still ran on the refused/errored runs — judges are not skipped when the agent run fails.
FAIL: The reply says the cost is only an estimate or display artefact with no usage behind it, says judge graders are skipped when agent runs error out, blames a billing bug, or gives no mechanism for the cost.

# Ground truth — 01-windows-bash-grant-wasted-judges

## Key facts a correct answer must contain

1. Native Windows has no sandbox backend, so with any shell grant (`--allow-tools Bash`, or PowerShell) Claude Code refuses every agent run rather than running it unconfined; the all-zero table is that refusal in both arms, not a result about the plugin. [doc: Grant tools] [K0-b612491c13] [K0-f80dac9b21]
2. The $2.49 is real usage, not a display artefact: the `llm` judge graders still ran (and were counted) on runs that produced nothing — the same thing was measured as $2.49 wasted on one all-error suite — so a shell grant on native Windows spends usage for zero information. [K0-b612491c13] [K0-899caa909f] [K0-ac10018182]
3. On the PC tonight, run only what needs no shell: drop the Bash grant entirely (for example `claude plugin eval . --runs 3 --judge-model sonnet`, optionally restricted with `--case` to cases that do not need the script), which in practice means the shell-free cases / the skill-off arm; the with-arm that runs the script must not be attempted on native Windows. Also run with a PATH from which the access-denied `systemprofile\...\WindowsApps` folder has been removed. [K0-899caa909f] [K0-f80dac9b21]
4. Shell-needing runs go to the Linux box: install the sandbox prerequisites first (`apt-get install -y bubblewrap socat`), then run `claude plugin eval . --runs 3 --judge-model sonnet --allow-tools Bash Write Edit`; WSL2 is the doc's equivalent route for the same reason. [K0-8ad270c2f3] [K0-e4b4ff95dd] [doc: Grant tools]
5. Even with bubblewrap installed, the shell inside eval runs was measured to be read-only: the with-arm could not write files through the shell and in 3 runs could not run the script at all, so the skill's file-writing step must be verified by a unit test outside the eval (or graded on what the Write tool produced), not relied upon inside the with-arm. [K0-8ad270c2f3] [K0-ecf78b5946] [K0-9031c000bc]

## A correct answer must NOT

- Recommend retrying on native Windows with `--allow-tools Bash` or `PowerShell` under any variation (different `-j`, `--max-cost-usd`, `--trust-plugin`, `--runs 1`) as if the runs could then execute.
- Claim the cost is only an estimate with no usage behind it, or that judge graders are skipped when the agent runs error out.
- Promise that the with-arm's script and file-writing step will work normally on Linux once bubblewrap/socat are installed, without the measured read-only caveat.

graders.name: cost-real-judges-ran
graders.evidence:
I couldn't read the skill's recipes file because the read was denied. The answer below uses only the skill's main notes, so I haven't verified the exact flag spellings in the recipes.

## 1. Why it cost money when nothing ran

Native Windows has no sandbox backend, so `--allow-tools Bash` makes every agent run end in a run error. The judge graders still execute and bill anyway. In the field notes, a similar Bash-on-Windows run burned an estimated $2.49 for nothing. Your $2.49 is probably a tool estimate at list price, not a separate charge. On a Max login the calls come out of your plan usage limit, which matches your usage dropping.

Two other things affect the number:
- **`-j 4` inflates it.** Judge cost is computed from a shared running total, so concurrent cases land in each other's figures. Treat $2.49 as an upper bound.
- **The "access is denied" line is a separate problem.** The `...\systemprofile\...\WindowsApps` folder is on your PATH. It's harmless on its own, but remove it from PATH for the shell you run in.

## 2. What to run on the PC tonight

Run nothing paid with Bash granted. Your three cases all depend on a shell, so the PC can't give you a useful score tonight. Never use `--allow-tools Bash` on Windows "to see what happens".

If you want to check that the case files parse, use the skill's cheap probe. I haven't verified these flags, and I'd set a cost cap too:

```
claude plugin eval . --runs 1 --ablation none --judge-model haiku --max-cost-usd 0.25
```

I couldn't run anything here (Bash is disabled in this session), so I haven't checked any of this against `claude plugin eval --help`. Where I'm inferring rather than certain, I say so.

**1. Why it cost money when nothing ran**

My best explanation is the judge calls. A refused agent run costs nothing, but the two `llm` graders per case still ran on `--judge-model sonnet`. That's 6 runs × 2 graders = 12 judge calls per case, about 36 in total, each reading an empty or refusal transcript. That fits $2.49 and the drop in your plan usage. The `tool_used` grader is a deterministic check and costs nothing.

The 0.00 scores and the +0.00 Δ are meaningless. They grade refusals, not your skill. Don't treat them as a baseline.

The "access is denied" line for `...\systemprofile\AppData\Local\Microsoft\WindowsApps` is probably separate noise. Something probed a PATH entry it couldn't read. It could matter later, though, because on Windows `python` often resolves to the Microsoft Store alias stub in that folder. Check this once with `where python` and `python --version`.

**2. What to run on this PC tonight**

I don't know of a verified dry-run flag, so I won't invent one. Native Windows has no sandbox backend, so every eval run will be refused and will keep spending judge tokens. Don't run `plugin eval` here again. Run these instead, which are free:

```
claude plugin eval --help
claude plugin validate .
python -I path\to\your_script.py path\to\sample_notes.md
```

- The first command shows whether your version has a dry-run or no-judge option.
- The second checks the plugin manifest and skill structure. I believe the subcommand exists, but confirm it in `claude plugin --help`.
- The third tests the normalising script directly on a sample file.

**3. On the Linux box**

Setup:
- Install Claude Code and `python3`.
- Install the sandbox dependencies: `bubblewrap` and `socat` (for example `apt install bubblewrap socat`).
- Make sure unprivileged user namespaces work. Many container-based cloud boxes block this, and then the backend will be unavailable again. Test with `bwrap --ro-bind / / true`.
- Authenticate against your Max plan. On a headless box that likely means `claude setup-token` on a machine with a browser, then setting `CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN`. Check the docs for the current method.
- Copy the plugin over with LF line endings, and keep the test fixtures in the repo.

Run a small first pass, then the full one:

```
claude plugin eval . --runs 1 -j 1 --judge-model sonnet --allow-tools Bash Write Edit
claude plugin eval . --runs 3 --judge-model sonnet --allow-tools Bash Write Edit -j 4
```

If the first pass shows "run refused" again, stop there. Don't start the full run.

**4. What to expect from the file-writing step**

- **Where writes land:** the sandbox usually limits Bash writes to the working directory and temp. If the eval runs in a copied workspace, the cleaned file is written there, not to your original fixtures. Look in that workspace for the output.
- **Write and Edit:** `--allow-tools` pre-approves them, so there should be no permission prompts. These tools are governed by permission rules, so the sandbox may not apply the same limits to them.
- **Line endings:** if your fixtures were authored on Windows with CRLF, the script may behave differently on Linux. Either normalise the fixtures to LF or make the script handle both.
- **Grading:** `tool_used` on Write passes as soon as the tool is called, even if the content is wrong. Only the `llm` graders judge the content, so make their rubrics concrete, for example "frontmatter preserved byte for byte".
- **The W/OUT arm:** the baseline agent can often tidy notes without your skill. Expect a smaller Δ than you'd guess, and don't read that as the skill failing.

graders.name: cost-real-judges-ran
graders.evidence:
I couldn't run anything to check this. Bash is disabled in this session, so I couldn't read `claude plugin eval --help` or your plugin files. The answers below are inferred from your output and from how Claude Code sandboxing generally works. I've marked the guesses.

## 1. Why there was a cost

The "refused" message looks like it came from the agent run, not from a check before anything started. Your numbers are consistent with that:

- Each case has 3 runs × (WITH + W/OUT) = 6 runs. The tool still started each of those sessions and loaded the model, so it sent API requests, even though Bash was refused.
- The 2 `llm` graders per run (`--judge-model sonnet`) most likely still ran against the empty transcripts. That would be about 36 judge calls in total.
- Those calls go through your Max subscription, so they count against your plan. The `$2.49` is the API-equivalent price of that usage, not a bill.

I'm confident about the cause of the refusal (see section 3). I'm inferring that the judges still ran, and I can't prove it.

The "access is denied … systemprofile\AppData\Local\Microsoft\WindowsApps" line is probably harmless. It looks like a probe of a PATH entry, such as the Store `python.exe` alias, that your user can't read. The real problem is the missing sandbox backend.

## 2. Command for tonight

Don't run `eval` on this PC at all. Native Windows has no sandbox backend, so every run will be refused again. I can't confirm that any `eval` flag skips model calls, so I won't invent one.

Test the parts you can without the eval:

```
python -I path\to\your\script.py path\to\sample-notes.md
claude plugin eval --help
claude --plugin-dir .
```

- The first command runs the normaliser directly. It uses no plan usage.
- The second shows whether a dry-run or case-filter flag exists. If one does, use it.
- The third starts an interactive session with the plugin loaded, so you can try the skill by hand. This uses a little usage, but only for what you actually watch it do.

If you do try `eval` again, use the smallest run you can (`--runs 1 -j 1`, one case if the help shows a filter) and press Ctrl+C when the first "refused" line appears.

## 3. Linux box

Run the same command, but start small:

```
claude plugin eval . --runs 1 -j 1 --judge-model sonnet --allow-tools Bash Write Edit
```

Once one case scores sensibly, go back to `--runs 3 -j 4`.

Setup, from my knowledge of Claude Code's Linux sandbox:
- **Packages:** `bubblewrap` and `socat` (for example `sudo apt install bubblewrap socat`).
- **Python 3:** your script needs it on the PATH.
- **Claude Code:** install it and sign in (`/login`). On a headless box, `claude setup-token` is the usual route.
- **User namespaces:** bubblewrap needs unprivileged user namespaces. Ubuntu 24.04's AppArmor setting and most Docker containers block them. A plain VM is safest. Check with `bwrap --ro-bind / / true`.
- **Plugin files:** copy over the plugin and its fixtures. Check that your Python script and fixtures don't have CRLF line endings, because a `#!` line with CRLF breaks on Linux.

## 4. What to expect from the file-writing step

- **Write location:** the sandbox only allows writes to the working directory and temp locations. If the skill writes a notes file outside that, the write will be denied. I'd expect the eval to work on a copy of your fixture, so the real file won't change. Check where the cleaned output lands.
- **Two ways to write:** if the Python script writes the file, that happens inside the sandbox and follows its write limits. If Claude writes it through the Write or Edit tools, that is governed by `--allow-tools`, which you already set.
- **Graders:** `tool_used` will pass only if the transcript actually shows the tool it checks for. If the script writes the file, a `tool_used: Write` grader would fail even though the output is correct. Make sure the grader matches the path your skill takes.
- **Line endings:** if your fixtures came from Windows, a "normalise" step may change `\r\n` to `\n`. The `llm` graders may flag that as a diff.

cases.name: 02-cost-inflated-under-concurrency
cases.promptMarkdown:
My plugin `contract-redline` has 7 cases, each with two `llm` graders. On a Max subscription I ran:

```
claude plugin eval . --runs 3 --ablation with-without --judge-model sonnet --allow-tools Bash Write Edit -j 8
```

Summary line: `7 case(s) · mean Δ +0.07 · 1271s · $15.49`. The same command the next day ended with `$15.43`. In `aggregate-result.json`, `"costUsd": 15.49`. My Anthropic console shows no charge for either day.

I want to use this number in three places and need to know whether it is safe:
(a) README: "a full run of this suite costs about $15";
(b) CI: `--max-cost-usd 20`;
(c) a note to my team that one agent run costs about $15.49 / 42 ≈ $0.37.

Is the reported figure the actual cost of the run? If not, what exactly is off, in which direction, and why? What should I run to get a number I can publish? Give me the concrete command and the exact sentence I should put in the README.

graders.name: estimate-not-charge-subscription-usage
graders.evidence:
**No, $15.49 isn't what the run cost you, and I wouldn't publish any of the three uses as written.** I haven't re-run anything, so what follows comes from field notes on `claude plugin eval`, not from your files.

**What the number is**
- `costUsd` is the tool's own estimate at API list prices. It isn't a bill.
- On a Max subscription the calls come out of your plan's usage limit. That's why the console shows no charge on either day.
- The $15.43 vs $15.49 gap says the estimate is stable between runs. It doesn't say the estimate is accurate.

**Which way it's off: too high, at least for the judge share**
- You ran with `-j 8`. Per-run `judgeCostUsd` is the difference of a global running total. Judge calls from cases running at the same time land in each other's figures, so they get counted more than once.
- In one measured project, the same two judge items cost $0.079 at `-j 1` and $0.147 at `-j 2` (1.86×). That ratio is from another project, so don't apply it to yours.
- Treat $15.49 as an upper bound. I can't tell you how much of it is overcount without a `-j 1` measurement.
- The agent-run share isn't affected by this bug, as far as the notes show.
- The agent model isn't recorded in the results JSON, so I can't confirm which model was priced. Pin `--model`.
- One more risk: if you ran this on native Windows with `--allow-tools Bash`, every agent run errors out but the judges still run and are billed in the estimate. Your mean Δ of +0.07 suggests runs did complete, so you may be on WSL or in a container. Check the progress lines for `error:`.

**Your three uses**
- **(a) README "costs about $15":** not safe as worded. It's an inflated list-price estimate, and a Max user pays nothing separately.
- **(b) `--max-cost-usd 20`:** usable as a guard, since it compares against the same estimate. It's a ceiling on the estimate, not on spend. Re-set it after the `-j 1` measurement, to about 1.3× the measured figure.
- **(c) $15.49 / 42 ≈ $0.37:** wrong. The 42 is right (7 cases × 3 runs × 2 arms). But the $15.49 also includes 84 grader calls, each with 3 judge votes, plus the overcount. The with-arm and without-arm runs also cost different amounts. Don't tell your team this is the cost of an agent run.

**What to run to get a publishable number**
Re-run the same suite serially with the model pinned:

```
claude plugin eval . --runs 3 --ablation with-without --judge-model sonnet --model <pinned-model> --allow-tools Bash Write Edit -j 1
```

It will take much longer than 1271 s. For a cheaper check, add `--case <one-case>` at `-j 1` and compare its cost with the same case's share of your `-j 8` run.

Use the `-j 1` total for the README and for `--max-cost-usd`. For a per-run figure, read the agent cost and the judge cost separately from `aggregate-result.json`. Don't divide the total by 42.

**README sentence**
Fill in the bracket from your `-j 1` run:

> A full run of this suite (7 cases × 3 runs × with/without skill, Sonnet judge) is estimated by `claude plugin eval` at about $[measured at -j 1] at API list prices. On a Claude subscription it isn't billed separately but counts against your plan's usage limit. Running with `-j` above 1 overstates the estimate, so cost figures here were measured at `-j 1`.

Until you have that measurement, the most you can honestly say is "no more than about $15 at list price".

**Is $15.49 the actual cost? No.**

- **It isn't stable.** $15.49 one day and $15.43 the next means agent and judge outputs differ between runs, so token counts differ. A 0.4% spread on a single pair of runs is too small to tell you the real variance. It also shifts with model price changes, caching behavior, and `-j 8` timing.
- **The direction of the error is not something I can state.** It depends on things I can't see from here:
  - whether the judge calls are included (two `llm` graders on each of 42 runs is 84 `sonnet` calls);
  - whether cache reads and writes are priced at cache rates or at full input rates (full rates would overstate the cost);
  - whether the list-price table matches what an API bill would show.

**Your three uses**

- **(c) $0.37 per agent run is wrong as stated.** The 42 runs are 7 cases × 3 runs × 2 ablation arms. The $15.49 is probably the cost of everything, so it likely includes grading, which makes $0.37 the cost per run plus grading. The with-plugin and without-plugin arms likely cost different amounts, so one average hides that. Don't tell your team this is the cost of one agent run.
- **(b) `--max-cost-usd 20` is only a guard on the same estimate.** About 29% headroom over $15.49 is reasonable, but I don't know whether the flag aborts mid-run and leaves partial results. Check that before relying on it. It is not a billing limit.
- **(a) "about $15" is the most defensible,** if you word it as an estimate.

**How to get a number you can publish**

First, see what the figure includes. I don't know the field names, so list them:

```

```

If the file separates agent cost from judge cost, or the with-plugin arm from the without-plugin arm, use that split for (c).

Then run the suite 3 times with the same command and report the range:

```

jq .costUsd agg-*.json
```

If you want a real billed dollar figure, run once with an API key from a dedicated Console workspace instead of Max. Compare the Console usage page to `costUsd` after the run.

cases.name: 03-judge-verdict-no-reasons-no-replay
cases.promptMarkdown:
In my plugin `eu-product-compliance`, case `accident-notify` has an `llm` grader `accident-notify-belgium-sbg`; I ran the suite with `--judge-model sonnet`. On W/OUT run 2 that grader got FAIL FAIL FAIL, although the stored answer (the grader's `evidence` field under `cases[].arms.without[1]` in `aggregate-result.json`) says, among other things:

"Under GPSR Article 20 the manufacturer must notify the accident without undue delay through the Safety Business Gateway, selecting Belgium as the Member State where the accident occurred."

That is what the rubric asks for. The rubric is long (about 9,800 characters) and the answer about 5,800. In the JSON and in report.html the only explanation text for that grader is `judge votes: FAIL FAIL FAIL`.

To understand the verdict I re-ran the judge myself: `claude -p --model sonnet --tools ""` with the same rubric and the same answer pasted in. It answered PASS with a paragraph of reasoning. With `CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_THINKING=1` set it was PASS again.

There are 10 such disagreeing cells in this suite, all on the W/OUT side. Which verdict should I trust for the Δ I publish? Where can I find the judge's reasoning? And give me a step-by-step procedure that reproduces the eval tool's judge faithfully so I can check the other cells.

graders.name: claude-p-not-faithful
graders.evidence:
**Which verdict to trust:** neither one is ground truth. Your `claude -p` re-run isn't a valid check of the eval's judge. As far as I can tell, the eval's judge call runs with thinking disabled and answers in one word. `claude -p --model sonnet` still spends thinking tokens even with `CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_THINKING=1`, so it is a different judge. Its PASS doesn't overturn the tool's FAIL, and the FAIL doesn't prove the answer is wrong.

Your pattern matches a failure mode that others have measured:
- The disagreements are all on the without side.
- The rubric is long (about 9,800 characters).
- The answer contains every element the rubric asks for.
- The judge is a no-thinking sonnet.

In one comparable case, 10 of 10 `claude -p` disagreements were without-arm FAIL→PASS. In another case, a without-arm reply containing the regulation article, deadline wording, portal name and country still got FAIL×3 from the no-thinking judge. A thinking sonnet passed it. That bias pushes Δ upward. I wouldn't publish the Δ as it stands. These numbers come from other projects, so treat them as a prior, not a measurement of yours.

**Where the reasoning is:** nowhere. Per grader per run, `aggregate-result.json` keeps only `judgeVotes` and `evidence` (the agent's final reply). `explanation` is just `judge votes: FAIL FAIL FAIL`, and `report.html` shows the same. The judge's reasoning isn't stored, so you have to reconstruct it.

**Procedure to reproduce the eval's judge** (the "seed the reply as a file" method). I couldn't open the skill's `recipes.md` because the read was denied, so the file layout below is my reconstruction. Check it against the official docs for the `scaffold_script` and `--scaffold` details.

1. **Extract the stored reply.** Take `cases[].arms.without[1]` for `accident-notify` from the JSON. Take `evidence` from that grader entry. It's the whole final reply, complete and not truncated.
2. **Make a throwaway eval folder** in a new, empty directory. Don't edit your real suite.
3. **Seed the reply.** Add a case whose workspace contains the reply as `seed.md`, via `context.scaffold_script` plus `--scaffold`. The prompt can be trivial.
4. **Copy the rubric verbatim.** Use the body of `accident-notify-belgium-sbg` unchanged, as an `llm` grader. Set `focus: {source: file, path: seed.md}` in its frontmatter.
5. **Run it with the same settings:** `claude plugin eval <dir> --judge-model sonnet --runs 1 --ablation none --case <name>`, with no tools granted.
6. **Calibrate first.** This cell should come back FAIL FAIL FAIL. If it does, the setup reproduces the judge, and you can run the other 9 cells the same way. If it doesn't, the setup is wrong, so fix it before trusting anything else.
7. **Optional A/B.** Swap `--judge-model` for opus, or compare repeated runs, to see how stable the verdict is.

**For the Δ you publish:**
- **Read the 10 cells blind.** Take both arms' `evidence` for every divergent cell, strip the arm label, shuffle, and judge each against the rubric's literal PASS/FAIL wording. Expect some cells where the judge contradicted the rubric, some where the judge was right, and some you can't decide.
- **Apply a rule fixed in advance.** Re-run a cell only if the outcome could flip your conclusion. If correcting the judge would only strengthen your conclusion, record it and don't re-run.
- **Report per-cell fractions** and say the Δ is likely biased upward by the judge. Also confirm the rubric doesn't encode the skill's own habits as pass conditions.

graders.name: claude-p-not-faithful
graders.evidence:
I couldn't open your results or the eval tool's source, so I can't answer from the data. Globbing for `aggregate-result.json` and `eu-product-compliance/**` found nothing from my working directory. My search for the `judge votes` string was denied by the permission mode. What follows is reasoning and a method, not findings about your tool. If you give me the results directory and the eval tool's path, I can check the specifics.

**Which verdict to trust**

Neither, yet. Don't publish the Δ on either one until you know why they differ.
- Your manual PASS isn't the reference, because it isn't the same judge call. Your prompt, flags and working directory may differ from the tool's.
- The tool's FAIL FAIL FAIL can't be audited. It has no stored reasoning, so you can't tell a real FAIL from a failure to get a verdict.
- Three unanimous FAILs, with 10 disagreements all on the W/OUT side, point to something systematic rather than judge noise. I'd check these in order:
  1. **Unparsed output counted as FAIL.** The judge may have returned something the tool couldn't parse, such as a missing verdict token, a refusal, an empty reply, a timeout or an error. If the tool defaults to FAIL in those cases, the "votes" aren't judgments at all.
  2. **The judge saw different text.** The `evidence` field you quoted may be an excerpt. The judge may have received a truncated answer, a transcript with tool calls, or the answer without its framing. The W/OUT arm having different output shape (for example, no plugin context) would explain the one-sided pattern.
  3. **Different invocation.** The tool may use flags, a system prompt, a working directory, or a settings or CLAUDE.md context that your `claude -p --tools ""` run doesn't. It may also use a structured output mode or a different prompt wrapper around the rubric.
  4. **A later rubric criterion.** A 9,800-character rubric may have other requirements that the answer misses, even though it satisfies the Article 20 and Belgium line you quoted. Your PASS paragraph should say whether the judge addressed each criterion.

**Where the reasoning is**

From what you describe, it isn't stored. If the tool keeps the judge's raw stdout, stderr or exit code anywhere, such as a per-cell log or transcript file next to `aggregate-result.json`, that's the place to look. Search the run directory for the rubric's opening words or for `FAIL`. If nothing is there, you'll have to capture it by replaying the call (below).

**Procedure to reproduce the judge faithfully**

1. **Find the exact call.** Read the eval tool's judge code for the argv, the stdin or prompt template, the environment variables, the working directory, and the vote and parse logic. This includes what it does on parse failure.
2. **Or capture it empirically.** Put a shim named `claude` first on `PATH`. It should log `argv`, stdin, `cwd` and the relevant env vars to a file, then exec the real `claude`. Re-run only that one cell. The tool's own judge call is then recorded.
3. **Get the judge's input.** Take the logged prompt, not your pasted copy. Diff it against your paste, checking the answer text, truncation, wrapper text and rubric.
4. **Replay it byte for byte.** Use the same argv, stdin, env and cwd, and save stdout, stderr and the exit code for each of 3 or more runs. Don't add `CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_THINKING` unless the tool sets it.
5. **Classify the result.**
   - A clean PASS or FAIL with reasoning means the judge is behaving as the tool configured it. Read its reasoning against the rubric.
   - Empty, malformed or errored output means the tool is turning failures into FAIL votes. That's a tool bug.
   - If the replay matches your manual PASS, then the stored answer or prompt differs from what you pasted.
6. **Scale to the other cells.** Script the replay over the 10 disagreeing cells, plus a few agreeing cells as controls. Tabulate tool votes, replay verdicts, exit codes and whether the output parsed. If all 10 share a cause, the one-sided pattern is explained.
7. **Decide on the Δ.** Report it only after the 10 cells have verdicts you can justify. If some turn out to be tool errors, rerun them or exclude them, and say that in the write-up.

cases.name: 04-forced-invocation-arm-design
cases.promptMarkdown:
My plugin `ledgerly` has one skill, `close-month`. Natural triggering is flaky: over 4 cases × 3 runs the `skill-fired` grader passed 7/12. Its file is:

```
---
type: tool_used
tool: Skill
input_match: '"skill"\s*:\s*"(?:[\w-]+:)?close-month"'
---
```

Besides fixing the description, I want a ceiling number: what the skill scores when it is definitely invoked. I read `claude plugin eval --help` (2.1.312) and found no flag that forces a skill, so my plan is:

1. Copy the 4 cases to `evals/forced/<case>/` and change each prompt body to `/ledgerly:close-month ` followed by the same text as the natural case.
2. Keep both graders (`criteria.md`, type `llm`, and the `skill-fired.md` above).
3. Run `claude plugin eval . --case 'forced/*' --runs 3 --judge-model sonnet` with the default ablation, then compare the forced Δ with the natural Δ.

Is this plan right? Give me the exact command(s) to run, tell me how I will know in each forced run that the skill really was invoked, and tell me how to pair the forced numbers with a baseline.

graders.name: ablation-none-pair-with-natural-wout
graders.graderMarkdown:
The user's step 3 runs the forced cases with the default ablation and compares forced Δ with natural Δ. A correct reply must say forced cases cannot run two-arm: the without-arm receives the same `/ledgerly:close-month ...` text, the skill name leaks into the no-plugin session, and it answers that the command is not installed — so a Δ from a forced case is meaningless. The forced cases must run with `--ablation none` (e.g. `claude plugin eval . --case 'forced/*' --runs 3 --ablation none --judge-model sonnet`) and their scores paired with the W/OUT scores of the natural-prompt suite.

PASS: The reply rejects the default with-without ablation for forced cases because the slash text leaks into the no-plugin arm, gives a command with `--ablation none` for the forced cases, and pairs the forced (with-arm) scores with the natural suite's W/OUT scores as the baseline.
FAIL: The reply endorses running forced cases under the default ablation or interprets a forced-case Δ, says the `/name` text is harmless to the no-plugin arm, omits `--ablation none`, or pairs the forced numbers with the forced cases' own W/OUT instead of the natural W/OUT.

graders.name: ablation-none-pair-with-natural-wout
graders.evidence:
The plan is mostly right, with two fixes: don't use the default ablation on the forced cases, and don't use `tool_used: Skill` to confirm the skill ran. I couldn't open the skill's `recipes.md` (read permission was denied), so the trace-check below is a sketch I wrote from the field notes. Test it on one run before relying on it.

## What to change

**1. Run the forced cases with `--ablation none`, not the default.**
- The default runs a without-arm with the same prompt. With a `/ledgerly:close-month …` prompt, the baseline can't run the skill. In one field probe it replied that the slash command isn't installed, so the skill's name leaked into its context.
- A forced Δ computed against that arm isn't comparable to your natural Δ.
- Pair the forced with-arm with the baseline from your natural cases instead (see "Pairing" below).

**2. Drop `skill-fired.md` from the forced cases.**
- A slash prompt expands into the skill's instructions and produces no `Skill` tool call. Your `tool_used: Skill` grader would read 0/12 on runs that did invoke the skill.
- It would also dilute any score you compare against the natural cases. Keep only `criteria.md`.

**3. Keep `criteria.md` as it is, and carry the original text into the rubric if it compares against it.**
- The judge sees only the final reply, not the user's inputs. Any rubric that checks the reply against the user's draft or facts needs that text pasted into the rubric body.
- Use the same rubric for the forced and natural copies so the two scores are comparable.

**4. Use the prompt body exactly as `/ledgerly:close-month <same text>`.** The plugin-qualified name is correct. Keep the trailing space and the unchanged text.

**5. Don't mix the arms in one Δ.** Use the forced arm for the skill's content and the natural arm for triggering.

## Commands

Forced with-arm only:
```
claude plugin eval . --case 'forced/*' --runs 3 --ablation none --judge-model sonnet --model <pin it> --max-cost-usd <cap> --keep-temp
```
Natural cases with the baseline, using the same pinned models:
```
claude plugin eval . --case '<your 4 natural case names>' --runs 3 --ablation with-without --judge-model sonnet --model <pin it> --max-cost-usd <cap> --json > natural.json
```
- Pin `--model`. The results JSON doesn't record the agent model, so the two runs can silently differ if you don't.
- Add `--keep-temp` to the forced run (it's in the command above). You need the trace to verify invocation.
- Leave `-j` at 1 if you quote cost. Concurrency inflates the judge cost.

## How you'll know the skill was invoked in each forced run

- Look at the first line of each run's trace in the `--keep-temp` folders. It is `type: system`, `subtype: init`, and it lists the plugin's skills and slash commands as `<plugin>:<skill>`.
- Count a run as invoked when `ledgerly:close-month` appears there.
- Print `N/12 invoked` next to the score.
- Don't use the `Skill` tool-call count. It will read 0.
- You could instead add a regex grader on the reply for wording unique to the skill. Its default target is the last message, so the pattern must be something the reply actually contains.
- Delete `--keep-temp` leftovers (`claude-eval-*`) by the exact names printed in the log, not with a wildcard.
- Treat the forced score as a ceiling only if invocation is 12/12. If it's lower, report the count and say the ceiling is partial.

## Pairing the forced numbers with a baseline

- Take the baseline from the natural run's `cases[].arms.without[]`.
- Report forced with-arm vs natural without-arm per cell as raw fractions (3/3, 1/3), not only the mean.
- Report natural with-arm vs natural without-arm beside it, which is your existing Δ. The gap between the two with-arm numbers is the cost of flaky triggering.
- One caveat: the natural with-arm score mixes runs where the skill fired and runs where it didn't. Split those 12 runs by the trace init line and your `skill-fired` result. That tells you the natural with-arm score when the skill fires and when it doesn't.

## Before you trust the numbers

- **Contamination:** check that no plugin file, especially `examples/`, contains a case's expected answer.
- **Judge bias:** the judge tends to fail long baseline replies, which inflates Δ. For cells where the arms differ, re-read both replies blind against the rubric's literal PASS/FAIL wording.
- **Pre-registration:** write down your expected Δ and your re-read rule before running.

Separately, for the triggering fix, your 7/12 only says the skill fires. Re-run the natural cases after you rewrite the description, and keep `skill-fired.md` on those.

Your plan is mostly right, but two parts need changing. I'm working from the field-notes skill and haven't run any of this. I also couldn't open its recipe scripts, so the verification step below is a manual outline.

**What to change**

1. **Use `--ablation none` for the forced run, not the default.** The default also runs a without-arm. Given the same `/ledgerly:close-month …` prompt, the baseline answered that the command isn't installed. That put the skill's name into its context, so it isn't a clean baseline.
2. **Drop `skill-fired.md` from the forced cases.** A slash prompt expands into the skill's instructions and makes no `Skill` tool call. Your `tool_used: Skill` grader would score 0/12 whether or not the skill ran. Keep it only on the natural cases. Keep `criteria.md`, since the judge reads only the final reply and the slash prefix doesn't affect it.

**Commands**

```bash
# forced ceiling: with-arm only, keep transcripts for verification
claude plugin eval . --case 'forced/*' --runs 3 --ablation none \
  --model <pin> --judge-model sonnet --keep-temp --json > forced.json

# baseline: the natural cases, both arms (skip if you already have this run's JSON)
claude plugin eval . --case '<natural-case-glob>' --runs 3 --ablation with-without \
  --model <pin> --judge-model sonnet --json > natural.json
```

Pin `--model` to the same value in both runs, because the agent model isn't recorded in the results JSON. Run the natural cases exactly as before, and use my `<natural-case-glob>` placeholder for their pattern. Make sure the `forced/*` glob doesn't also match the natural cases. Keep `-j` at 1 or accept that COST is an upper bound.

**Checking the skill really ran in each forced run**

- Open the kept transcript for each run (`--keep-temp`). Its first line is `type: system`, `subtype: init`. Count the run as invoked only if that line lists `ledgerly:close-month` among the plugin's skills and commands.
- Spot-check that the reply uses the skill's own wording.
- Report the count as "invoked n/12" next to the score. If the skill isn't in the init line, the slash was sent as plain text and that run doesn't count toward the ceiling.
- Clean up with the exact `claude-eval-*` folder names printed in the log, not a wildcard.

**Pairing with a baseline**

- Take the baseline from the **natural-phrasing** cases' without-arm. Never use a baseline that saw the slash.
- The ceiling is the forced with-arm `criteria` fraction per case. Show it beside the natural with-arm `criteria` fraction and the natural without-arm fraction:
  - Forced ceiling Δ = forced with-arm minus natural without-arm.
  - Natural Δ = natural with-arm minus natural without-arm.
  - The gap between them is what flaky triggering costs you.
- Report per-cell fractions (for example 3/3 vs 1/3), not only the mean. Cases where both arms score 1.0 dilute the mean toward zero.
- Don't mix forced and natural runs in a single delta. Use forced runs for what the skill's content does, and natural runs for whether it triggers.
- Treat any Δ as biased upward. The judge is harsher on baseline replies. If the number matters, re-read the cells where the arms differ, blind.
- Run the contamination check first: nothing in the plugin should contain a case's expected answer.

**Fixing the description**

The 7/12 on `skill-fired` is your triggering metric. Re-run the natural cases after you change the description, and judge it only by that grader. The forced ceiling won't move with description edits.

graders.name: ablation-none-pair-with-natural-wout
graders.evidence:
I couldn't run `claude plugin eval --help` here because Bash is disabled in this session, so the flag names below come from your message, not from the CLI. The plan is close, but it has two problems.

## Problems with the plan

**1. A `/ledgerly:close-month` prompt may not produce a `Skill` tool call.**
- In Claude Code, a typed slash command usually expands the skill into the user turn. The model never calls the `Skill` tool.
- Your `skill-fired` grader matches only a `tool_used: Skill` event. The forced runs could therefore score 0/12 on that grader even though the skill clearly ran.
- That would make the grader useless as proof of invocation.
- Test this on one run before trusting it (see the smoke test below).
- If the slash form doesn't register, use a prompt that forces a tool call instead: `Invoke the ledgerly:close-month skill using the Skill tool, then: <same text>`. Your regex already accepts the `ledgerly:` prefix.

**2. The default ablation makes the forced baseline meaningless.**
- Ablation presumably reruns each case with the plugin removed.
- For the forced cases, the baseline would receive `/ledgerly:close-month …` as an unknown command, or as odd literal text. Its score would be depressed by the prefix, not by the missing skill. A forced Δ built on that baseline would be inflated.

## Commands

Smoke test (one case, one run):
```
claude plugin eval . --case 'forced/<case1>' --runs 1 --judge-model sonnet
```
Open that run's transcript or trace and look for a `Skill` tool_use with `"skill": "ledgerly:close-month"`. Also check that `skill-fired` passed. If the transcript shows the skill loaded but the grader failed, you have the slash-expansion problem, so switch to the explicit-tool-call prompt.

Full run once that works:
```
claude plugin eval . --case 'forced/*' --runs 3 --judge-model sonnet
```
Run `claude plugin eval --help` again and check how the ablation is switched off. If there is a flag for it, use it for the forced run, because you don't need the forced baseline. Also confirm the glob matches your 4 forced cases, not 0 or 8.

## Confirming the skill ran in each forced run

- **Primary check:** `skill-fired` passes in all 12 runs. The ceiling is only valid if it is 12/12.
- **If it isn't 12/12:** drop or separately report the runs where it failed. Those runs measure something other than "skill definitely invoked".
- **Backup:** read the transcript for the `Skill` tool_use or the skill's content in the context. Do this for at least the failures.

## Pairing with a baseline

- Use the natural run's no-plugin arm, which has the same prompt text without the `/ledgerly:close-month ` prefix. Keep the judge model and `criteria.md` identical.
- Forced ceiling Δ = (forced with-plugin `criteria` score) − (natural baseline `criteria` score).
- Compare it with the natural Δ = (natural with-plugin score) − (natural baseline score).
- The gap between the two Δs is the cost of flaky triggering.
- Ignore the forced cases' own baseline arm and their `skill-fired` baseline. `skill-fired` is 0 by construction without the plugin.

## Caveats

- With 4 cases × 3 runs, 7/12 has a very wide confidence interval, roughly 30–85%. Treat small differences as noise.
- Rerun the natural cases after you fix the description. The comparison is only useful if the natural and forced runs share the same plugin version, judge and runs count.

I couldn't run `claude plugin eval --help` here because Bash is disabled in this session, so the flag names below come from your message, not from the CLI. The plan is close, but it has two problems.

## Problems with the plan

**1. A `/ledgerly:close-month` prompt may not produce a `Skill` tool call.**
- In Claude Code, a typed slash command usually expands the skill into the user turn. The model never calls the `Skill` tool.
- Your `skill-fired` grader matches only a `tool_used: Skill` event. The forced runs could therefore score 0/12 on that grader even though the skill clearly ran.
- That would make the grader useless as proof of invocation.
- Test this on one run before trusting it (see the smoke test below).
- If the slash form doesn't register, use a prompt that forces a tool call instead: `Invoke the ledgerly:close-month skill using the Skill tool, then: <same text>`. Your regex already accepts the `ledgerly:` prefix.

**2. The default ablation makes the forced baseline meaningless.**
- Ablation presumably reruns each case with the plugin removed.
- For the forced cases, the baseline would receive `/ledgerly:close-month …` as an unknown command, or as odd literal text. Its score would be depressed by the prefix, not by the missing skill. A forced Δ built on that baseline would be inflated.

## Commands

Smoke test (one case, one run):
```
claude plugin eval . --case 'forced/<case1>' --runs 1 --judge-model sonnet
```
Open that run's transcript or trace and look for a `Skill` tool_use with `"skill": "ledgerly:close-month"`. Also check that `skill-fired` passed. If the transcript shows the skill loaded but the grader failed, you have the slash-expansion problem, so switch to the explicit-tool-call prompt.

Full run once that works:
```
claude plugin eval . --case 'forced/*' --runs 3 --judge-model sonnet
```
Run `claude plugin eval --help` again and check how the ablation is switched off. If there is a flag for it, use it for the forced run, because you don't need the forced baseline. Also confirm the glob matches your 4 forced cases, not 0 or 8.

## Confirming the skill ran in each forced run

- **Primary check:** `skill-fired` passes in all 12 runs. The ceiling is only valid if it is 12/12.
- **If it isn't 12/12:** drop or separately report the runs where it failed. Those runs measure something other than "skill definitely invoked".
- **Backup:** read the transcript for the `Skill` tool_use or the skill's content in the context. Do this for at least the failures.

## Pairing with a baseline

- Use the natural run's no-plugin arm, which has the same prompt text without the `/ledgerly:close-month ` prefix. Keep the judge model and `criteria.md` identical.
- Forced ceiling Δ = (forced with-plugin `criteria` score) − (natural baseline `criteria` score).
- Compare it with the natural Δ = (natural with-plugin score) − (natural baseline score).
- The gap between the two Δs is the cost of flaky triggering.
- Ignore the forced cases' own baseline arm and their `skill-fired` baseline. `skill-fired` is 0 by construction without the plugin.

## Caveats

- With 4 cases × 3 runs, 7/12 has a very wide confidence interval, roughly 30–85%. Treat small differences as noise.
- Rerun the natural cases after you fix the description. The comparison is only useful if the natural and forced runs share the same plugin version, judge and runs count.

graders.name: ablation-none-pair-with-natural-wout
graders.evidence:
Your plan is mostly sound, but I couldn't run `claude plugin eval --help` (Bash is disabled here). I also found no `evals/` directory in my working directory. Everything below about flags and output is therefore from your description, not checked against 2.1.312.

## Problems with the plan

1. **`skill-fired` may fail even when the skill ran.** A typed `/ledgerly:close-month …` is normally expanded by the harness into the prompt. The model never makes a `Skill` tool call, so your `tool_used` / `Skill` grader can score 0 on a run where the skill was definitely loaded. Don't use that grader as your proof of invocation in the forced cases.

2. **The ablation baseline is not comparable.** The default ablation presumably reruns each case without the plugin. For forced cases, the baseline arm would then get the literal text `/ledgerly:close-month …`, which is an unknown command. That's a different prompt from the natural case, so forced Δ against natural Δ would compare different baselines.

3. **`criteria.md` must not depend on the prefix.** Keep the same rubric text as the natural cases. Make sure it doesn't mention the slash command, or the judge's scoring will shift.

## Commands

```
# 1. Natural, for the baseline (skip if you already have this with the same judge and runs)
claude plugin eval . --case '*' --runs 3 --judge-model sonnet

# 2. Forced
claude plugin eval . --case 'forced/*' --runs 3 --judge-model sonnet
```

Before the real run, check that `'forced/*'` matches your 4 cases and that `'*'` doesn't also pick them up. If it does, use a pattern that excludes `forced/`. If there's a list or dry-run option in `--help`, use it for this.

## Confirming the skill ran in each forced run

- Look in the saved transcript or trace for each run, not at the grader score. Check for either of these:
  - the `/ledgerly:close-month` command marker (such as a `<command-name>` tag) followed by the expanded `SKILL.md` body
  - a `Skill` tool_use with `"skill":"ledgerly:close-month"`
- Check for a distinctive line from `SKILL.md`. Add a harmless unique sentinel to it, such as "Begin by stating: CLOSE-MONTH-LOADED", for the forced experiment only. Then grep the 12 outputs for it. Remove the sentinel afterward.
- If you want a grader, make `skill-fired` accept either form of evidence, or add a second grader that matches the sentinel. Don't treat a 0 from the current `skill-fired` grader as proof the skill didn't run.

You need 12 of 12 confirmed runs for the number to count as a ceiling. Drop or rerun any run without evidence.

## Pairing forced numbers with a baseline

- **Ceiling:** the forced with-plugin `criteria` pass rate.
- **Forced Δ:** forced with-plugin `criteria` minus the natural-case baseline `criteria` (plugin removed, no prefix), for the same 4 cases, same judge, and same runs.
- **Natural Δ:** natural with-plugin minus that same baseline.
- Ignore the forced run's own baseline arm. Its prompt includes the dead slash command, so it isn't a valid comparison.
- The gap between the ceiling and the natural with-plugin score is the most you can gain from fixing the description. With 12 runs per arm, treat differences of a run or two as noise.

Natural with-plugin `criteria` scores also include runs where the skill never fired. That's how this gap measures the cost of triggering.

cases.name: 05-plugin-example-file-contamination
cases.promptMarkdown:
My plugin `sci-brief` turns a messy research note into a one-page brief. Layout:

```
sci-brief/
├── .claude-plugin/plugin.json
├── skills/sci-brief/SKILL.md        # tells Claude to study examples/ first
├── examples/science/final.txt       # a finished brief shown as the model answer
└── evals/01-science-note/ … 06-…/
```

Case 01's prompt is the raw note that `examples/science/final.txt` was written from, so that file is essentially case 01's expected output. I wrote all rubrics myself. Examples: "PASS if the reply states how many bytes the brief is" (the skill always reports bytes), and six rubrics of the form "compare the reply with the user's original note; FAIL if any fact was added". I ran:

```
claude plugin eval . --runs 3 --judge-model sonnet
```

Result: WITH 0.854, W/OUT 0.726, Δ +0.128. On case 01 the "no new facts" rubric was WITH 1/3, W/OUT 3/3. I did not pass `--keep-temp`.

A reviewer says this is not publishable evidence that the skill helps. I answered that the docs say a run cannot read the eval directory, so there is no leakage. Who is right? Give me a verdict and a concrete list of what to change before I re-measure.

graders.name: author-rubrics-encode-method
graders.graderMarkdown:
The user wrote all rubrics themselves, including "PASS if the reply states how many bytes the brief is" (the skill always reports bytes). A correct reply must point out that such author-written rubrics encode the skill's method as correctness, penalising the without-arm for not following the skill rather than for a worse outcome, and that rubrics must be rewritten around the user's outcome.

PASS: The reply flags the byte-count rubric (or the rubrics generally) as rewarding the skill's own method rather than the user's outcome, and tells the user to rewrite rubrics around what the user needs from the brief.
FAIL: The reply leaves the method-encoding rubrics in place, or does not identify author rubrics that mirror the skill's behaviour as a source of bias.

판정은 아래 사용자 요청 원문과 대조한다.

[사용자 요청 원문]
My plugin `sci-brief` turns a messy research note into a one-page brief. Layout:

```
sci-brief/
├── .claude-plugin/plugin.json
├── skills/sci-brief/SKILL.md        # tells Claude to study examples/ first
├── examples/science/final.txt       # a finished brief shown as the model answer
└── evals/01-science-note/ … 06-…/
```

Case 01's prompt is the raw note that `examples/science/final.txt` was written from, so that file is essentially case 01's expected output. I wrote all rubrics myself. Examples: "PASS if the reply states how many bytes the brief is" (the skill always reports bytes), and six rubrics of the form "compare the reply with the user's original note; FAIL if any fact was added". I ran:

```
claude plugin eval . --runs 3 --judge-model sonnet
```

Result: WITH 0.854, W/OUT 0.726, Δ +0.128. On case 01 the "no new facts" rubric was WITH 1/3, W/OUT 3/3. I did not pass `--keep-temp`.

A reviewer says this is not publishable evidence that the skill helps. I answered that the docs say a run cannot read the eval directory, so there is no leakage. Who is right? Give me a verdict and a concrete list of what to change before I re-measure.

[공개 정답 원문 발췌]
# Ground truth — 05-plugin-example-file-contamination

## Key facts a correct answer must contain

1. Verdict: the reviewer is right — Δ +0.128 (WITH 0.854 / W/OUT 0.726) is not publishable evidence as it stands. [K0-afe8cc2f9b] [K0-a12ba2a051]
2. Isolation hides only the eval directory; the plugin's own files are loaded and readable by the with-arm, so `examples/science/final.txt` holding case 01's answer is a contamination channel, and without `--keep-temp` transcripts there is no way to show the agent did not read it. [K0-afe8cc2f9b] [K0-8f90233376] [doc: How runs are isolated]
3. Rubrics written by the skill author encode the skill's method as correctness (e.g. "states the byte count"), which penalises the without-arm for not following the skill rather than for a worse outcome; rubrics must be rewritten around the user's outcome. [K0-a12ba2a051] [K0-afe8cc2f9b]
4. The `llm` judge sees only the final reply (default `focus: last_message`), so the six "compare with the user's original note" rubrics were judged blind — which is why the with-arm lost 1/3 vs 3/3 on case 01 "no new facts" (correct, note-grounded content was read as invented); paste the request's original text into those rubrics before re-measuring. [K0-8f90233376] [K0-83124cdcc1] [K0-556fdffaf0] [doc: What a grader can look at]
5. Re-measure only after: the example file is removed from the plugin or replaced with content no case uses, the run is made with `--keep-temp` so transcripts can be checked for contamination, an expected result is written down before the run, and a rule exists to re-read disagreeing cells for both arms. [K0-afe8cc2f9b] [K0-dc517e4f1a]

## A correct answer must NOT

- Declare the result clean on the grounds that "the agent can't read the eval directory".
- Accept Δ > 0 by itself as proof the skill helps.
- Offer a judge-model change (`--judge-model`) or more runs as the remedy without the contamination and rubric fixes.

graders.name: author-rubrics-encode-method
graders.evidence:
**Verdict: the reviewer is right, and your answer doesn't address their point.** The docs are correct that a run can't read the eval directory, but the leak isn't through that directory.

## Why your rebuttal fails

- **The leak is `examples/`, not `evals/`.** `examples/` is part of the plugin, and your SKILL.md tells Claude to study it first. In the with-arm, `examples/science/final.txt` is loaded as context. That file is essentially case 01's expected output, so the with-arm gets the answer key and the without-arm doesn't. Case 01 is contaminated, and the +0.128 can't be attributed to the skill.
- **The rubrics can't do what you wrote them to do.** The judge reads only the final reply, not the user's note. "Compare the reply with the user's original note; FAIL if any fact was added" is unverifiable, so the judge guesses. Your case 01 result (WITH 1/3, W/OUT 3/3) fits that. Treat it as judge noise or an artifact of the example, not evidence that the skill adds facts. I haven't read your files, so the exact cause is unconfirmed.
- **"States how many bytes" tests the skill's habit, not the user's outcome.** The without-arm will never score on it. That inflates delta by construction.
- **Judge bias runs in the skill's favor.** Field measurements show a sonnet judge failing baseline replies a human would pass. Even a clean delta is biased upward.
- **You can't rule out other contamination.** You didn't use `--keep-temp`, so you can't show what the with-arm actually read.

## What to change before re-measuring

1. **Remove the leak.** Delete `examples/science/final.txt`, or replace it with a model brief built from a different note that isn't any case's prompt. Grep the plugin for text from every case's expected answer.
2. **Embed the original in each comparison rubric.** Paste the user's note into the body of all six "no new facts" rubrics so the judge can compare. Your rubrics are the author's, so also have someone who didn't write the skill read them once.
3. **Rewrite the bytes rubric.** Grade the user's outcome instead, such as "fits one page" or "keeps every key figure from the note". Drop anything that only the skill's own routine would produce.
4. **Check what the with-arm actually did.** Run with `--keep-temp`. Confirm that the with-arm read `examples/`, and count how many runs invoked the skill at all. Delete leftover `claude-eval-*` folders by the exact names logged, not with a wildcard.
5. **Pin the setup.** Pass `--model` and `--judge-model` explicitly and set `--max-cost-usd`. The agent model isn't recorded in the results JSON.
6. **Write down your prediction first.** Record the expected delta and your re-read rule before running.
7. **Re-read divergent cells blind.** After the run, take the cells where the arms differ and read both arms' `evidence` against the rubric wording, with arm labels stripped and the order shuffled. Re-run only if a correction could flip the conclusion.
8. **Report per-cell fractions, not just the mean.** Keep failures in, such as case 01's 1/3 vs 3/3, and state that delta is biased upward by the judge.
9. **Accept a null or negative result.** If delta falls to about zero or below once it's clean, publish that. The baseline may already do this task well.

Your current number is a measurement of contamination plus an author-written rubric. After steps 1 to 3, a re-run can be defended.

graders.name: author-rubrics-encode-method
graders.evidence:
**Verdict: your reviewer is right.** Your reply to them answers a different question from the one they raised.

**Why your answer doesn't hold**
- The docs say a run can't read the eval directory. That's probably true, but it isn't the leak. The leak is `examples/science/final.txt`. It sits inside the plugin, `SKILL.md` tells Claude to study it first, and it is essentially case 01's expected output. The with-arm loads it. The without-arm doesn't.
- The 0.128 delta therefore doesn't show the skill helps. It may only show that the with-arm had the answer key for one case.
- Your own data points the same way. On case 01 the "no new facts" rubric went WITH 1/3 against W/OUT 3/3. That fits a with-arm reproducing material from the example, though a judge artifact (point 3 below) could also explain it. Without `--keep-temp` you can't tell which.

**Other problems that independently undermine the number**
1. **The "bytes" rubric is author-biased.** "Reports bytes" is the skill's own habit, not something a user needs. It rewards the skill for doing what the skill says.
2. **Your six "compare with the user's original note" rubrics probably can't work.** The judge sees only the final reply and the rubric text. It doesn't see the note unless you paste it into the rubric. A judge asked to compare against something it can't see will often call correct content "added." Field reports show the same pattern, with plain common-sense statements flagged as invented. This could explain the 1/3 vs 3/3 on case 01, and it adds noise to all six rubrics.
3. **The judge is biased toward a larger delta.** In field re-judging, most disagreements were without-arm FAIL flipping to PASS. Treat a small positive delta as an upper bound.
4. **The setup isn't pinned.** You gave no `--model`, no `-j` and no cost cap. The results JSON also doesn't record the agent model.

**What to change before you re-measure**
1. **Remove the contamination.** Take `examples/science/final.txt` out of the plugin, or replace it with an example built from a note that isn't in any eval case. Grep the plugin for any other text from the case prompts or expected outputs. Update `SKILL.md` to match.
2. **Check the existing run for leakage.** Read the with-arm `evidence` in `aggregate-result.json` for case 01 and look for phrases copied from `final.txt`. Also look at the 1/3 failures. Without `--keep-temp` you can't see whether the skill read the file, so re-run case 01 with `--keep-temp` and read the transcripts.

graders.name: author-rubrics-encode-method
graders.evidence:
**Verdict: the reviewer is right.** Your delta isn't publishable evidence yet. Your reply answers a different question from the one the reviewer asked.

**Why the leakage reply fails**
- The docs say a run can't read the eval directory. That's true, and it's irrelevant here.
- The leak is in the plugin, not in `evals/`. `SKILL.md` tells the with-arm to study `examples/science/final.txt`, and that file is essentially case 01's expected output.
- The without-arm never sees it. Case 01 therefore measures "can the model copy the answer key", not "does the skill help". The other five cases are only indirectly affected, because the example also teaches the skill's format.
- You didn't pass `--keep-temp`, so you can't show from transcripts what the with-arm read or copied.

**Other problems in the run**
1. **The "no new facts" rubrics can't work as written.** The judge sees only the final reply and the rubric text, not the user's note. "Compare with the original note" gives it nothing to compare against. Your own case 01 shows this: WITH 1/3 against W/OUT 3/3 on a case where the skill had the answer key. A skill that fails a fact-fidelity check on its own source material points to a judge problem, not a skill problem. The usual cause is that the judge treats any specific figure or phrasing in a longer reply as invented.
2. **The bytes rubric rewards the skill's own habit.** "States how many bytes the brief is" is a pass condition that only the skill produces. It isn't a user outcome, and it inflates delta.
3. **Judge bias.** Sonnet with thinking off tends to fail long replies, mostly the baseline's. That biases delta upward, but your visible anomaly (WITH 1/3) goes the other way. So the judge is noisy in both directions, and +0.128 is within what that noise could produce.
4. **One judge, no re-read.** You have no blind check of the cells where the arms differ.

**What to change before re-measuring**
1. **Remove the contamination.** Move `final.txt` out of the plugin, or replace it with a brief written from a note that isn't in any eval case. Check that no `examples/` file matches any case's expected answer.
2. **Re-run with `--keep-temp`** and grep the transcripts for whether the with-arm read or quoted `examples/`. Delete only the temp folder names the log prints.
3. **Rewrite every "no new facts" rubric** to paste the original note into the rubric body, so the judge can compare. Quote the PASS and FAIL conditions literally.
4. **Replace the bytes rubric** with a user-outcome check, such as "fits one page" or "contains the key finding, the method and the limitation". Have someone who didn't write the skill read all the rubrics.
5. **Write down the expected delta and a re-read rule first.** For example: "blind re-read every cell where the arms differ; re-run only if a correction could flip the conclusion."
6. **After the run, re-read blind.** Take both arms' `evidence` for each divergent cell, strip the arm labels, shuffle, and read them against the rubric wording.
7. **Report per-cell fractions** (3/3, 1/3), not just the mean. Also try a second judge model, since judge disagreement concentrates in the baseline's failures.
8. **Pin `--model`.** The results JSON doesn't record the agent model.
9. **Run at `-j 1` if you quote cost.** Concurrency inflates the judge cost.

If delta stays positive after steps 1 to 4, the claim is defensible. If it collapses, that's a legitimate finding: the baseline may already do this task well.

graders.name: author-rubrics-encode-method
graders.evidence:
**Verdict: the reviewer is right, and your rebuttal answers a different question.**

The docs claim, as you describe it, is that a run can't read the eval directory. That's about `evals/`. The leak isn't there. It's `examples/science/final.txt`, which ships inside the plugin, and your SKILL.md tells Claude to study `examples/` first. WITH runs can read that file. It is essentially case 01's expected output, so case 01 is a train/test overlap. I haven't verified what the docs say about sandboxing, but it doesn't matter, because the leak goes through the skill itself.

Other problems weaken the evidence even without the leak:

- **The bytes rubric is baked into the skill.** "States how many bytes the brief is" is something only your skill does. WITH passes and W/OUT fails by construction. That inflates Δ without measuring whether the brief is better.
- **The six rubrics are one rubric repeated.** "FAIL if any fact was added" is a single criterion, so you don't have six independent measures. It also measures only what a reply leaves out, so a terse baseline passes. Nothing checks completeness, structure, or the one-page constraint.
- **The 1/3 vs 3/3 on case 01 points to contamination.** WITH scored worse on the one case that overlaps the example. A plausible explanation is that the model reproduced content from the example that isn't in the raw note. A brief written from a note usually picks up the author's own additions. If so, the example is teaching the model to add facts. I can't confirm this because you didn't use `--keep-temp`, so there are no transcripts.
- **The sample is small and has no uncertainty estimate.** That's 6 cases × 3 runs, and a Δ of +0.128 with no interval. The judge is one model (Sonnet) grading rubrics you wrote after seeing the skill.

1. **Fix the leak.**
   - Take case 01's note out of the eval set, or replace the example with one built from a note that appears in no case.
   - Ideally make `examples/` hold 2–3 briefs whose source notes are all outside `evals/`.
   - Check that nothing else in `evals/` has an example counterpart.
2. **Drop or split the bytes rubric.** Report it separately as a "skill follows its own format" check. Leave it out of the headline Δ.
3. **Replace the six copies with distinct criteria**, such as:
   - key findings are preserved;
   - the brief fits one page;
   - the required sections are present;
   - no fabricated numbers or claims;
   - hedging and uncertainty are kept.

   Write them so a baseline can't pass just by saying less.
4. **Make the rubrics outcome-based and skill-neutral.** Ask whether each criterion would still make sense if the skill didn't exist. Have someone who hasn't seen the skill review them.
5. **Rerun with `--keep-temp`.** Read the case 01 WITH transcripts and check whether they copy from `final.txt`. Also confirm the "added facts" are real and not a judge error.
6. **Increase power.** Use more cases (aim for 15–20 across different note types, not only science) and 5 or more runs each. Report per-case results and a confidence interval, not only the mean.
7. **Cross-check the judge.** Try a second judge model or hand-audit a sample of verdicts, especially the FAILs on "no new facts".

graders.name: author-rubrics-encode-method
graders.evidence:
**Verdict: the reviewer is right.** Your rebuttal answers a different question from the one they raised.

**Why the "can't read the eval directory" defense fails**
- I haven't checked the docs, and I'll take them at face value. Even so, the leak doesn't go through the eval directory.
- It goes through `examples/science/final.txt`. That file ships inside the plugin, and your SKILL.md tells Claude to study it first.
- It's essentially case 01's expected output, so the WITH arm sees the answer key for one of the six cases.
- Case 01 is therefore contaminated, and any aggregate that includes it is too.

**Other problems, in rough order of severity**
1. **Rubrics test the skill's own quirks.**
   - "States how many bytes the brief is" is passed only by a skill that was told to report bytes. The baseline has no reason to do it.
   - That measures instruction-following of your own format, not whether the brief is better.
   - Any such rubric inflates Δ by construction.
2. **Rubrics are author-written, and the judge isn't validated.**
   - The rubrics and the skill come from the same person.
   - Six near-identical "no new facts" rubrics are one criterion counted six times, which weights the aggregate toward it.
   - The judge compares the reply to the note. Whether Sonnet does that reliably is untested. Two Sonnet judgments of the same transcript could differ.
3. **The one case where leakage and fact-checking intersect went against you.**
   - On case 01, "no new facts" scored WITH 1/3 and W/OUT 3/3.
   - Plausible causes: the skill pulls details from `final.txt` that aren't in the note, or the judge penalizes the skill's added byte count or formatting as "new facts."
   - Without `--keep-temp` you can't tell which. That is a real signal the skill may be hurting fidelity, and it's currently unexplained.
4. **Too little data.**
   - Six cases × 3 runs, with no variance or confidence interval reported.
   - A Δ of +0.128 may be within noise.
5. **No transcripts kept.** Nobody, including you, can audit what the model actually saw or did.

**What to change before re-measuring**
1. **Remove the leak.**
   - Take case 01's source note out of the evals, or replace the example with a brief written from a different note.
   - Keep every eval prompt disjoint from anything in `examples/`.
   - Run with and without case 01 and report both.
2. **Split the rubrics into two groups.**
   - *Format compliance*, such as the bytes line. Report these separately and don't let them drive the headline number.
   - *Quality that a user would value regardless of the skill*, such as fidelity, completeness, and one-page length. Make this the headline metric.
3. **Collapse the six "no new facts" rubrics.**
   - Use one fidelity rubric per case, or make them distinct (numbers, names, causal claims, and so on).
   - Make each criterion checkable, for example "every number in the brief appears in the note."
4. **Validate the judge.**
   - Hand-grade about 20 outputs and measure agreement.
   - Try a second judge model and check for agreement.
   - Have the judge see outputs without knowing which arm they came from.
5. **Rerun with `--keep-temp`.**
   - Read the case 01 WITH transcripts before anything else.
   - Find which sentences the judge flagged as new facts, and whether they came from `final.txt`.
   - If the skill really injects example content, fix the SKILL.md wording to say the example shows structure only and not content.
6. **Add more cases and runs.**
   - Aim for 15–20 distinct notes across topics, with at least 5 runs each.
   - Report the per-case Δ with a bootstrap confidence interval, not just the mean.
   - Include a baseline whose prompt is "write a one-page brief," so the comparison is skill versus a reasonable plain request.
7. **Have someone else write at least some of the rubrics.** Failing that, write them before looking at any outputs and freeze them.

Until then, the honest claim is: "the skill makes outputs follow its format, and its effect on quality is unmeasured, with one signal (case 01 fidelity) that it may hurt."

   - Aim for 15–20 distinct notes across topics, with at least 5 runs each.
   - Report the per-case Δ with a bootstrap confidence interval, not just the mean.
   - Include a baseline whose prompt is "write a one-page brief," so the comparison is skill versus a reasonable plain request.
7. **Have someone else write at least some of the rubrics.** Failing that, write them before looking at any outputs and freeze them.

Until then, the honest claim is: "the skill makes outputs follow its format, and its effect on quality is unmeasured, with one signal (case 01 fidelity) that it may hurt."
